entry.title: Prepare for the removal of WMIC from Windows 11
entry.content: The Windows Management Instrumentation command-line (WMIC) utility has been removed from Windows 11, version 24H2 and later. It’s no longer available as a Feature on Demand on these versions. WMI itself remains supported and unaffected. Organizations should identify applications, scripts, deployment tools, and monitoring systems that use WMIC and migrate them to PowerShell or supported WMI programming interfaces. Learn more at Windows Management Instrumentation command-line (WMIC) removal from Windows.

entry.title: New PowerShell scripts to manage Windows settings backup data

entry.title: Task Manager features for visibility into AI workloads

Specifically, per-process activity for the neural processing unit (NPU) and graphics processing unit (GPU) neural engine now appear on the Processes and Performance tabs, alongside other familiar data. A new blog article illustrates three use cases for IT professionals, developers, and power users. Read it in Task Manager features for visibility into AI workloads.

entry.title: Windows device recovery in 2026: A guide for IT pros

entry.title: 60-Day Reminder: AD FS DKM container ACL hardening begins in October 2026
entry.content:
Windows updates released in October 2026 will begin Enforcement mode for AD FS Distributed Key Manager (DKM) container ACL hardening, a change designed to address the elevation of privilege vulnerability documented in CVE-2026-56155. Organizations using AD FS should use the remaining Audit mode period to review DKM container permissions and address compatibility issues before enforcement begins.

With the October 2026 Windows security update, supported versions of Windows Server will run remediation by default unless administrators explicitly opt out. Windows Server 2012 and Windows Server 2012 R2 still require manual remediation and will not be automatically remediated during Enforcement mode.

For more details, see: CVE-2026-56155: AD FS Distributed Key Manager container ACL hardening.

entry.title: Enforcement phase for Kerberos RC4 protections begins with the July 2026 Windows security update
entry.content:
The July 2026 Windows security update enables Enforcement mode across Windows domain controllers for Kerberos RC4 protections related to CVE‑2026‑20833. Domain controllers enforce updated behavior for service account ticket issuance. RC4-based Kerberos tickets are restricted under this enforcement model, and AES-based encryption is expected for supported configurations. This change helps reduce reliance on legacy encryption methods and aligns Kerberos authentication with current security standards.

Earlier phases introduced audit and compatibility checks beginning in January 2026, followed by default AES-only behavior and optional rollback controls in April 2026. As of the July 2026 Windows security update, Audit mode and the temporary RC4DefaultDisablementPhase registry setting are removed, and Enforcement mode is the only supported configuration.

This final phase blocks Kerberos service ticket requests that rely on RC4 or other legacy encryption types when no explicit configuration is present, helping reduce exposure to credential recovery attacks associated with weaker encryption.

If your organization still depends on RC4-based Kerberos scenarios, those workloads might experience authentication failures after installing the July 2026 Windows security update. Review all service accounts, applications, and non-Windows integrations to confirm support for AES-based encryption and address any remaining dependencies.

Learn more at: How to manage Kerberos KDC usage of RC4 for service account ticket issuance changes related to CVE‑2026‑20833.

entry.title: Windows settings backup policy is becoming a new default
entry.content:
Starting with Windows 11, version 26H2, the default behavior of the Windows settings backup policy will shift from disabled to enabled. Default-on applies only to eligible devices and only when admins haven't explicitly set the policy. Explicit enablement and disablement settings are always honored. Restore behavior is unchanged: it remains admin-controlled and isn’t enabled by default.

This change makes backup a baseline resilience capability, so you can restore users' apps, settings, and Microsoft Store app list easier after a device reset, replacement, or upgrade. Admins keep full control through Microsoft Intune, Group Policy, or other MDM solutions. Learn more in Windows settings backup becoming a new resilience baseline.

entry.title: Task Manager adds NPU columns and neural engine visibility across views
entry.content:
If your PC has a neural processing unit (NPU), Task Manager now gives you a fuller picture of AI compute. Neural engines appear on the Performance page for the first time on both NPU and graphics processing unit (GPU). Additionally, a new set of NPU columns mirrors the GPU columns that already existed. This gives you a clear view of which apps are using the neural engines on your NPU and GPU. Use this information to pinpoint what's affecting performance and battery life. More generally, see whether your apps are making use of the efficient AI hardware that your PC provides. This is available on eligible devices that install the June non-security update or later. 
 
The NPU and NPU Engine columns on the Processes and Users pages show how much of the NPU each process and user is consuming and which engine is driving it. All four new columns (NPU, NPU Engine, NPU Dedicated Memory, and NPU Shared Memory) are available on the Details page. To add any of the new columns, right‑click (or select and hold) a column header in Task Manager, then select them from the menu.  
 
The existing GPU Engine column is also updated to surface the neural engine. As a result, neural workloads running on a GPU's hardware neural engine now appear under GPU Engine on the Processes, Users, and Details pages.

entry.title: Point-in-time restore for Windows is generally available
entry.content: Point-in-time restore is a new, built-in Windows recovery feature that lets users roll their Windows PC back to a previous state in minutes. The goal is to help organizations minimize downtime and simplify remediation without lengthy troubleshooting or full device rebuilds. To get started, install the June 2026 Windows non-security update and learn more about Point-in-time restore for Windows.

entry.title: 30-Day Reminder: Final deployment phase for Kerberos RC4 hardening begins with the July 2026 Windows security update
entry.content:
Windows updates released in July 2026 will begin the final deployment phase of protections designed to address a Kerberos information disclosure vulnerability (CVE‑2026‑20833). This phase completes the transition from legacy encryption types such as RC4 by removing Audit mode and leaving Enforcement mode as the only supported behavior for Kerberos RC4 usage on Windows domain controllers.

Beginning with the July 2026 Windows security update, environments with remaining RC4 dependencies might experience authentication failures unless those dependencies are remediated or explicitly configured before the update is installed.

If your organization relies on service accounts, applications, or devices that still depend on RC4‑based Kerberos service tickets, now is the time to address those dependencies before Enforcement mode becomes mandatory. Continue monitoring the System event log for Kerberos‑related audit events and use those signals to identify and remediate RC4 reliance or insecure encryption configurations.

Organizations should also validate interoperability for non‑Windows Kerberos implementations and services before broadly deploying the July 2026 update, as Audit mode rollback will no longer be available once this phase begins.

For more information about the vulnerability, rollout timeline, recommended preparation steps, and configuration options, see How to manage Kerberos KDC usage of RC4 for service account ticket issuance changes related to CVE‑2026‑20833 and CVE‑2026‑20833.

entry.title: Upgrade to Windows Server 2025, now via Windows Update
entry.content:
Windows Server supports several methods for moving to a newer version, including in-place upgrade. This method installs a newer version of Windows Server over the existing one, keeping your settings, server roles, features, and data.

Windows Update can now be used to perform a Windows Server feature upgrade. This in-place upgrade can help move Windows Server 2022 or Windows Server 2019 installations to Windows Server 2025, following the same process used to download monthly updates through Windows Update and without the need for installation media. Upgrading helps keep your servers secure, supported, and able to use the latest features and performance improvements.

Please note that several steps are necessary in order to enable the offering, including update requirements and the addition of registry keys. Learn about the in-place upgrade paths by version, prerequisites, and restrictions at Opt-In Windows Server 2025 Feature Update from the WS 2022 and WS 2019 Settings Dialog.

entry.title: Second deployment phase for Kerberos RC4 hardening begins with the April 2026 Windows security update
entry.content:
Windows updates released in April 2026 and later begin the second deployment phase of protections designed to address a Kerberos information disclosure vulnerability (CVE‑2026‑20833). This second phase continues the shift away from legacy encryption types such as RC4 by moving toward stronger default ticket behavior. After installing the April 2026 update, domain controllers default to supporting Advanced Encryption Standard (AES‑SHA1) encrypted tickets for accounts that do not have an explicit Kerberos encryption type configuration.

If your organization relies on service accounts or applications that depend on RC4-based Kerberos service tickets, now is the time to address those dependencies to avoid authentication issues before the Enforcement phase begins in July 2026. Microsoft recommends continuing to monitor the System event log for Kerberos-related audit events and identify and address misconfigurations or remaining dependencies, then enabling enforcement when warning, blocking, or policy events are no longer logged.

See How to manage Kerberos KDC usage of RC4 for service account ticket issuance changes related to CVE-2026-20833 and CVE‑2026‑20833 to learn more about the vulnerability, timelines, recommended preparation steps, and configuration options to ensure compliance before Enforcement mode begins in July 2026.

entry.title: Remote Desktop adds new safeguards for connections opened from RDP files
entry.content:
Starting with the April 2026 Windows security update, Remote Desktop adds new safeguards to help reduce phishing attacks that misuse Remote Desktop (.rdp) files. These attacks attempt to trick devices into connecting to attacker‑controlled systems and sharing local resources without clear visibility. To address this, a new security dialog appears before any connection is made, showing the remote computer address, publisher information (when available), and any requested access to local resources. All requested settings are disabled by default and must be explicitly enabled. A one‑time security warning also appears the first time an RDP file is opened. This change helps make potentially risky connections more visible and intentional, without affecting connections that are started manually in the Remote Desktop app.

Organizations that build or deploy custom Remote Desktop clients are encouraged to review their handling of RDP file–based connections. For more information, including detailed explanations of the new dialogs, redirection behavior, and available admin and developer options, see Understanding security warnings when opening Remote Desktop (RDP) files.

entry.title: Windows Deployment Services (WDS): Hands-free deployment hardening (Phase 2)
entry.content:
As announced in January 2026, the Unattend.xml file used in hands‑free deployment poses a vulnerability when transmitted over an unauthenticated RPC channel. Beginning with the April 2026 security update, the second phase of hardening changes for CVE-2026-0386 is now in effect. These changes make hands‑free deployment disabled by default to enforce secure behavior.

IT admins can override the secure‑by‑default setting to keep Unattend.xml‑based hands‑free deployments working, but this is not recommended. This is not a secure configuration. IT admins should migrate to alternate options and disable hands-free deployment to enhance security. For detailed guidance see: Windows Deployment Services (WDS) Hands‑Free Deployment Hardening Guidance.

entry.title: Hardening administrative actions: Windows imaging, cloning, and auth workflows

entry.title: Prepare devices for successful updates with Windows Autopatch update readiness
entry.content: Windows Autopatch update readiness helps IT admins proactively identify and resolve issues that can block Windows updates before deployment. It provides visibility into device readiness across the Microsoft Intune-managed Windows fleet and surfaces actionable insights to reduce update failures and manual troubleshooting. By shifting update management from reactive to proactive, it helps improve update success rates and strengthen overall fleet reliability.
